clinicalPearls: Accumulation of chyle within the pericardial space, producing a characteristically milky effusion rich in triglycerides and chylomicrons
May be primary (idiopathic, from abnormal lymphatic communication with the pericardium) or secondary to thoracic surgery, trauma, malignancy, mediastinal irradiation, or lymphangiomatous disorders
Often accumulates slowly and may be asymptomatic, but a large or rapidly forming effusion can cause tamponade
The diagnosis is confirmed by analysis of aspirated fluid showing a milky appearance, high triglyceride content, and chylomicrons
Imaging with lymphangiography or lymphoscintigraphy can localise the abnormal thoracic-duct or lymphatic connection in primary disease
Initial management combines pericardial drainage with measures to reduce chyle flow, such as a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides or bowel rest
Persistent or recurrent leakage may need ligation of the thoracic duct, a pericardial window, or pericardiectomy, sometimes with lymphatic embolisation
reference.pathophysiology: Chylopericardium arises when lymph rich in triglyceride-laden chylomicrons drains abnormally from the thoracic duct or its tributaries into the pericardial sac. In primary disease this reflects congenital or acquired abnormal lymphatic channels communicating with the pericardium, sometimes with reflux from the thoracic duct; in secondary disease the duct or its branches are disrupted by surgery, trauma, tumour, or radiation. The accumulating chyle raises intrapericardial pressure and, if large or rapid, impairs cardiac filling to cause tamponade, while chronic loss of chyle can deplete fat-soluble nutrients, protein, and lymphocytes.
additionalDifferentials: Serous pericardial effusion from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Pericardiocentesis with fluid analysis for a milky appearance, triglyceride level, and chylomicrons
Echocardiography to size the effusion and assess for tamponade
Cardiac CT or MRI to characterise the effusion and search for a mediastinal cause
Lymphangiography or lymphoscintigraphy to identify the abnormal lymphatic communication
Investigation for underlying malignancy or lymphatic disorder when secondary disease is suspected
redFlags: Cardiac tamponade from a large or rapidly accumulating chylous effusion
Recurrent reaccumulation after drainage indicating an unresolved lymphatic leak
Features suggesting an underlying mediastinal malignancy or lymphangiomatosis
Nutritional and immune depletion from chronic high-volume chyle loss
reference.prognosis: Primary chylopericardium often responds to dietary measures and drainage but can recur and require surgical or interventional treatment, whereas the outlook in secondary disease is largely determined by the underlying cause.
pitfalls: Mistaking chylous fluid for pus and missing the diagnosis without triglyceride analysis
Confusing chylopericardium with a pseudochylous cholesterol effusion
Draining the effusion without addressing the ongoing lymphatic leak, leading to recurrence
Overlooking an underlying malignancy or lymphatic disorder in secondary cases
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases
management: Pericardial drainage by pericardiocentesis for a large or symptomatic effusion, with emergency drainage for tamponade
Reduction of chyle flow with a low-fat diet enriched in medium-chain triglycerides, or bowel rest with parenteral nutrition
A somatostatin analogue such as octreotide to reduce lymphatic flow in persistent leakage
Lymphangiography with thoracic-duct embolisation, or surgical thoracic-duct ligation with a pericardial window or pericardiectomy, for refractory or recurrent disease
Identification and treatment of an underlying cause in secondary disease, such as malignancy or a lymphatic disorder
Monitoring of nutritional, immune and fat-soluble vitamin status given ongoing chyle loss
Cardiothoracic and cardiology referral with echocardiographic surveillance for reaccumulation and tamponade
